tagline: A direct highway crosses red hills between Coldwater and Medicine Lodge
intro: The Gypsum Hills Scenic Byway follows U.S. 160 for 42 miles between Coldwater and Medicine Lodge. Kansas Tourism highlights the buttes, canyons, mesas and sinkholes as unusual features of the Great Plains. Here the terrain rolls through red-tinted sediments, with small, steep canyons in the surrounding Red Hills. The red comes from oxidized iron in deposits laid down during the Permian Period. Gypsum left by shallow waters that repeatedly flooded and dried later dissolved underground, creating sinkholes. Wildflowers add another source of color along the route in spring.

U.S. 160 was extended into Kansas between 1930 and 1931, before the direct alignment between these towns was built. The numbered highway once took a longer route between the two towns, turning north toward Wilmore and passing through Sun City and Lake City. Between 1941 and 1944, a new alignment gave U.S. 160 a direct east-west course from Coldwater to Medicine Lodge.

Traveling east, begin at Coldwater, where U.S. 183 provides access to the byway. Stay on U.S. 160 across the Gypsum Hills toward Medicine Lodge. Kansas Tourism lists interpretive sites west of Medicine Lodge, including one on the south side of the highway. The drive ends at Medicine Lodge, where U.S. 160 meets U.S. 281.

moments.title: Coldwater
moments.text: Coldwater became the Comanche County seat in 1885, the year after six men from Harper County laid out the town and named it for Coldwater, Michigan. The first post office opened on October 17, 1884, during the town’s first year. Its courthouse tells a later chapter. A fire destroyed the earlier wood-frame courthouse in 1921; the replacement was built in 1927. Routledge & Hertz designed the four-story masonry building in the Classical Revival style, using buff brick with limestone trim. The county courthouse is at 201 South New York Avenue.

moments.title: Carrie Nation House
moments.text: Carrie Nation lived in this small brick house on Fowler Avenue from 1889 to 1902. In Medicine Lodge she organized a local branch of the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union and campaigned to enforce Kansas’s ban on liquor sales. Her protests escalated into attacks on saloons, including three in nearby Kiowa. At Kiowa, Nation threw rocks she called “smashers” to destroy a saloon’s stock. The house became a National Historic Landmark in 1976. Beside it is a reproduction stockade, built in 1961; the original stockade was larger and stood northeast of this site, nearer the town center.

moments.title: Medicine Lodge
moments.text: Near Medicine Lodge, three treaties signed in October 1867 assigned southern Plains tribes to smaller reservations in Indian Territory. The United States negotiated with the Kiowa, Comanche, Plains Apache, Southern Cheyenne and Southern Arapaho. The treaties called for surrender of traditional territories in exchange for smaller reservations and allowances of food, clothing and equipment. The Indian Peace Commission’s 1868 report concluded that the U.S. government and its representatives had contributed to warfare by failing to fulfill legal obligations. The town’s commemorative pageant began in 1927 and has been held every three years since 1961.
